Scarlet-chested sunbirds (Chalcomitra senegalensis) emerge from eggs incubated at an average temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C] after a developmental period of approximately 14.3 days [ab = approximately 14.3 days]. This incubation duration, recorded in a captive breeding colony, is consistent with values reported for other small nectivorous passerines of comparable egg size. Freshly hatched nestlings exhibit a modest initial wet weight of just 1.47 grams [Ww0 = 1.47 grams], reflecting the altricial state typical of passerine chicks. This body mass at emergence is substantially lower than the ultimate wet weight attained by adult females, which reaches 8.2 grams [Wwi = 8.2 grams] in fully grown, reproductively mature individuals. The nearly six-fold increase in mass from hatching to adulthood underscores the rapid growth trajectory that characterizes this species during the nestling phase, driven by intensive bi-parental provisioning of insect prey and nectar.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, specifically 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], fledging occurs at 17 days after hatching [tx = 17 days after hatching]. The achievement of first flight at this age marks the transition from the nestling stage to the fledgling phase, wherein juveniles remain dependent on parental care for an additional period as they refine their foraging skills. Documented ages at fledging are uniform across broods, indicating a canalized developmental schedule. In comparison to congeneric sunbird species that inhabit cooler montane environments, the nestling period of Chalcomitra senegalensis is relatively abbreviated, a pattern potentially linked to elevated ambient temperatures that accelerate metabolic processes. Following departure from the nest, the young birds continue to be fed by both parents while gradually learning to extract nectar from tubular flowers and capture small arthropods.

Gonadal maturation in this species proceeds at a measured pace, with puberty occurring at 51 days after hatching [tp = 51 days after hatching] when maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The onset of reproductive activity, however, is deferred considerably relative to the attainment of sexual maturity. First successful breeding events are typically recorded at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], also under the same thermal conditions at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This substantial lag between physiological readiness and actual reproductive effort is common among small passerines, likely reflecting the time required to establish a territory, secure a mate, and accumulate sufficient body condition to support egg production. Field observations from West African populations confirm that year-round breeding is possible in regions with consistent rainfall, though peaks in nesting activity coincide with flowering periods of major nectar sources.

Female reproductive output in this species is characterized by modest clutch sizes. Each nesting attempt yields two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], and females typically complete approximately 2.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2.5 clutches per year] when food availability is adequate. This annual fecundity is intermediate relative to other members of the Nectariniidae, balancing the energetic demands of egg production with the need for sustained parental care over multiple broods. The maximum recorded longevity for Scarlet-chested sunbirds is 8.2 years [am = 8.2 years] under conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This lifespan, documented through mark-recapture studies in Senegal, is comparable to that reported for other medium-sized nectarivores and likely reflects the trade-off between high metabolic rates associated with nectarivory and the relatively low extrinsic mortality faced by a territorial, long-lived species.

Resting metabolic measurements conducted under thermoneutral conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] reveal that Scarlet-chested sunbirds consume oxygen at a rate of 43 milliliters per hour [JOi = 43 milliliters per hour]. This basal metabolic rate, obtained from flow-through respirometry on post-absorptive individuals during their inactive phase, aligns with the elevated metabolic demands typical of nectarivorous birds that sustain high activity levels throughout the day. The combination of a relatively rapid developmental schedule, moderate reproductive output, and extended lifespan positions Chalcomitra senegalensis as a species with life-history traits attuned to the seasonal predictability of its savanna and woodland habitats. Continued monitoring of populations across their range will be essential to assess how ongoing habitat fragmentation and shifts in flowering phenology influence these demographic parameters.
